books.title: The 5 Love Languages
books.author: Gary Chapman
books.description: A simple framework for understanding how different people give and receive love.
ideas: People feel love differently
The five love languages are words of affirmation, quality time, gifts, acts of service and physical touch. Most of us have one or two that matter most.
Speak their language, not yours
We tend to show love in the way we want to receive it. If your partner values acts of service, a heartfelt card might not land as much as doing the dishes.
Keep the love tank full
When people feel loved in their own language, they handle stress and conflict better. Small daily gestures add up.
Love is a choice
Early infatuation fades. Lasting love comes from choosing to care for someone in ways that matter to them.

books.title: Attached
books.author: Amir Levine & Rachel Heller
books.description: How attachment theory explains the way we behave in romantic relationships.
ideas: Three attachment styles
Secure people are comfortable with closeness. Anxious people crave it and fear losing it. Avoidant people value independence and pull away when things get close.
Needing others isn't weakness
Depending on a partner is part of being human. Secure relationships let both people be more independent, not less.
The anxious-avoidant trap
Anxious and avoidant partners often attract each other, then trigger each other's fears in a painful cycle.
Effective communication
Saying what you need clearly and calmly shows you who can meet those needs, and helps a good partner do so.

books.title: The Seven Principles for Making Marriage Work
books.author: John M. Gottman & Nan Silver
books.description: A relationship researcher's evidence-based guide to what makes couples last.
ideas: The four horsemen
Criticism, contempt, defensiveness and stonewalling predict break-ups. Contempt, treating your partner as beneath you, is the most damaging.
Turn toward bids
Partners constantly make small bids for attention: "Look at that bird." Responding with interest, even briefly, builds connection over time.
Love maps
Strong couples know each other's worlds: worries, friends, dreams. Keep updating your map by asking questions.
Five to one
Stable couples have roughly five positive interactions for every negative one during conflict. Kindness doesn't need to be grand, just frequent.
Some problems are permanent
Many disagreements never fully go away. Successful couples learn to talk about them with humour and acceptance instead of gridlock.

books.title: The Art of Loving
books.author: Erich Fromm
books.description: A psychologist argues that love is a skill to be learned, not a feeling we fall into.
ideas: Love is an art
Like music or painting, love requires knowledge, practice and effort. We focus on being lovable, and neglect learning to love.
Love is active
Love is giving, not just receiving: care, responsibility, respect and knowledge of the other person.
Mature love keeps two people whole
Immature love says, "I love you because I need you." Mature love says, "I need you because I love you."
Self-love isn't selfishness
Respecting and caring for yourself is the ground from which you can love others well.

books.title: The Good Life
books.author: Robert Waldinger & Marc Schulz
books.description: Lessons from the Harvard Study of Adult Development, which has followed lives for over 80 years.
ideas: Relationships keep us healthy
In the longest study of adult life, the quality of people's relationships predicted their health and happiness in old age better than wealth or fame.
Loneliness is a health risk
Chronic loneliness is linked to poorer health and shorter lives. Social connection is as important as diet and exercise.
Social fitness
Relationships need regular exercise too. Reach out, check in and make time, or connections slowly weaken.
Small moments matter
A chat with a neighbour or barista counts. Brief, warm interactions boost mood and sense of belonging.
